title: Model Carving: Training Transformers That Optimize Their Own Topology
text: Machine learning has largely kept separate the choice of architecture and the process of training. A classic Transformer, for instance, trains a fixed set of attention and MLP sublayers at every layer, in the same order, and optimizes the weights within. This uniformity is a convention rather than a principled design choice, and it is likely suboptimal: the best architecture for a given task may be smaller, more efficient, and far from uniform. We believe that, ideally, training itself should shape the model's topology. To this end, we introduce Model Carving, which learns both a Transformer's weights and its architecture in a single run. By applying learnable, scalar gates to each sublayer, we allow the training loss to remove the model's own components during training -- freeing a smaller heterogeneous network inside. We evaluate Model Carving by pre-training standard Transformers from 140M to 2.7B parameters and looped Transformers from 140M to 1.3B. At equal training compute, carved models reach a lower validation loss than dense models trained with up to 1.7 times more compute. Furthermore, carved models also outperform size-matched models produced by pruning or distillation, suggesting that the best way to obtain small models for edge devices is to carve them during training, not to compress a large one afterwards. This advantage both grows with scale and carries over to downstream tasks such as few-shot evaluation and generation. Because the removed sublayers no longer run, carved models also cost up to 34% fewer FLOPs per token and decode up to 1.6 times faster without cost in quality. Our results show that architecture, like weights, should be learned and not fixed in advance, and that inside every large transformer is a smaller, faster, stronger one waiting to be carved out.

title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning
text: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the π_{0.5} baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the π_{0.5}. Project page: https://refocus-robotics.github.io.

title: Seeing Is Locating: Spatial Awareness and Geographic Bias in Decision Language Models
text: Decision models, which output probability distributions over candidate labels instead of generating text, are increasingly used as classifiers and evaluators for inputs associated with real-world locations. However, it remains unclear whether they can leverage spatial context and whether their predictions are geographically biased. We introduce GeoDecisions, a multimodal benchmark for evaluating the spatial awareness and geographic bias of decision models. GeoDecisions comprises two tasks: (1) geo-aware image classification, and (2) location rating on objective and subjective topics. Evaluating six decision models against supervised task-specific models, we find that spatial awareness requires vision: textual coordinates alone provide insufficient context for classifying everyday photos and satellite images. We also find substantial geographic bias. On everyday photos, despite achieving higher accuracy, open-weight decision models exhibit more spatially clustered errors than supervised models. Moreover, across all five subjective topics, every decision model gives lower ratings to locations with lower socioeconomic conditions. Finally, we propose a training-free method that combines decision models with a location prior to improve their spatial awareness without substantially increasing performance bias. Our code is available at https://github.com/cruiseresearchgroup/GeoDecisions.

title: Degradation of Language Models under Controlled Load: Synchronization, Rule Execution and Misfires on the Background
text: As the load grows, a language model makes more and more errors, but different processes stand behind this decline in quality. The model may lose the correspondence with the source text, it may keep its place in the text but execute a rule wrongly, or it may change a word that no rule concerns. In this work the degradation of a model under controlled load is separated into these three components: synchronization, rule execution and misfires. The load is set by rules that replace one word with another in a meaningless text, and each kind of load (the text length, the position of a word in the answer, the replacement density, the number of rules and the place of a rule in the list) is set separately. The alignment of the answer with the reference makes it possible to follow the outcome of every word, and a statistical model that takes into account that the spread of difficulty between requests itself depends on the load restores, for each component, the laws of its dependence on every kind of load. These laws make up the passport of a model. The paper presents the method of the separation, the principles of constructing the laws and the passports of seven models built by this method; the separation opens the way to studying the fine structure of the behavior of a neural network.

title: Foresight Forcing: Learning Spatial Foresight for Robotic Manipulation
text: Robotic manipulation policies can improve action prediction by anticipating how objects move and how their spatial relationships change. World Action Models (WAMs) learn to predict future visual observations, but their training objectives typically leave the underlying 3D geometric transitions implicit. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Foresight Forcing (F^{2}), a WAM that learns a spatial transition representation from changes in a pretrained 3D feature space. During training, a frozen 3D foundation model extracts patch-wise feature differences from aligned current and future observations that provide dense supervision for geometry-aware feature transitions. We distill these targets into spatial transition queries, which are progressively refined from the current observation, language instruction, and proprioceptive state, and use them alongside current visual features to generate actions. At deployment, the policy predicts the queries without future observations or the 3D teacher. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin2.0 demonstrate strong manipulation performance and improved robustness, including 95.01% average success on RoboTwin2.0 Full. On six real-world manipulation tasks, F^{2} achieves a mean task score of 85.8%.

title: Small Learned Projections for Semantic-Reversal-Aware Retrieval with Spectral Acceleration: A Four-Domain Empirical Study
text: Dense-embedding retrievers can fail adversarially: when a query is answered by a document A and reversed by a near-copy B that differs from A by a small meaning-changing edit (a "trap"), raw cosine over E5-Large-v2 places B in the top-10 for 82-100% of queries at a pool of 5,000. We study two things. First, a small learned projection W: R^1024 -> R^d (d in {11, 32}), trained by a deterministic recipe on a declared set of cases, that suppresses the trap: for the declared cases, HN@10 = 0.0000 (no trap in the top-10) in all twelve (domain, pool-size) settings across four independent domains (legal, medical, patent, financial) and pools up to 100,000, while the correct paraphrase is retained for 93-99% of cases, under exact nearest-neighbour search. Second, a boundary-conditioned accelerator that serves the projection at that scale: an acceleration of spectral graph retrieval (SpectRAG) that replaces a dense eigendecomposition with a boundary-value solve, holding HN@10 = 0.0000 at n = 100,000 in every domain and retrieving the ~300-query suite in 0.6-1.1 s (~2-4 ms per query on average). Because the lens's output is the stored representation (a few floats per document), a hardened, specialised index per domain or tenant is ~90x smaller and dimension-proportionally faster than the full embedding, making many small declared indexes a practical alternative to one large vector store. The claim is scoped to the declared cases on the measured pools, with no probabilistic bound; the correct-answer rate drops for a reworded query against an unchanged corpus (about 0.79, trap suppression still holding). A projection transfers only partly to other domains, which we report in full. The recipe, lenses, trap sets and evaluation harness are released under AGPL-3.0; the accelerator's implementation is a reserved commercial component, and every HN number is reproducible under exact search.

title: RoMo Hands: A Large Scale Richly Organized Text to Hand Motion Dataset
text: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.

title: EEGJev: A System One Decision Model and Benchmark for Multi-Task EEG Question Answering
text: A single electroencephalographic (EEG) recording can support multiple decoding tasks. Fixed-label tests cannot show how EEG foundation models handle changing questions or options. We introduce EEGJev, a fast decision model that scores candidate answers in one pass. Our benchmark, EEGJev-Bench, covers six question types across 19 public EEG sources. We held the recording and options fixed while switching between questions about attributes paired during training, such as facial expression and the hand participants were asked to use. Across 13 test sources, EEGJev selected a label for the requested attribute with 99.70% accuracy (49.20% under uniform choice). Balanced accuracy for the specific answer was 62.04%. Its 95th-percentile response time was shorter than NeuroLM's on matched validation questions answered individually. EEGJev lets users switch decoding targets by changing the question. With EEGJev-Bench, researchers can test whether new decoders follow the question more reliably, identify the correct answer more often, or both.

title: Evaluating Memanto on DolphinBench for AI Agents
text: Memory benchmarks built on question answering tell an agent which fact to recall. Workplace requests often leave that need implicit: to post an update in the team's channel, an agent must work out which channel from earlier interactions and use it in a tool call. We evaluate Memanto, a memory agent that ranks memories with an information-theoretic relevance score, on DolphinBench, which tests memory through 600 simulated workplace tasks, each validated as requiring memory. Running in the Hermes agent harness with GPT-6-Luna and at most 6 iterations per conversation, Memanto completes 503 tasks (83.83%). The strongest configuration reported by the benchmark's authors, Mem0 with GPT-5.6-Luna and up to 60 iterations, completes 424 (70.67%). Memanto's run also has the lowest total cost (10.86, against 61.48 for the cheapest reported run) and the shortest median task latency (15.32s). Grading uses the benchmark's own judge, but the agent model differs, so these results compare complete systems. The memory system affects both whether an agent completes such tasks and what completion costs.

title: DetourBench: Trajectory-Level Evaluation of Interactive Agents with Exact Minimum-Action Bounds
text: Benchmarks judge language-model agents mainly by whether they reach the correct final state, not by how they got there. Endpoint scoring cannot separate an agent that retrieved exactly the evidence a decision required from one that read most of the environment, nor an agent that never located the evidence from one that stopped a single action short. Settling this needs a reference cost, and authored solutions establish only that a task is solvable, not that no shorter route exists. We present DetourBench, which constrains the environment until that minimum is computable. Each task is a finite, partially observable transition system with unit-cost accesses whose resources become globally addressable after discovery. Exhaustive search yields the full-information minimum action count L_0 with a replayable witness; from graph-recoverable terminal states it also yields exact residual work R_T, which separates an episode that stopped one access short from one that wandered, while an irreversible wrong commitment is recorded as having no finite residual distance rather than assigned one. Success, attainment, residual progress, and normalized detour are reported separately. Across 375 scored episodes --- five model endpoints, 25 integrated tasks, three repeats --- success ranges from 58.7% to 96.0% while conditional attainment ranges from 0.803 to 0.890 and orders the models differently. Among recoverable failures, residual work separates near-complete trajectories from costly incompletion and from irreversible commitment. We open-source the instances, oracle witnesses, and evaluation harness at https://github.com/DatagridsAI/DetourBench.

title: CARE-3D: Reinforcement Learning for Evidence Grounded Agentic Reasoning in Situated 3D Scenes
text: Situated 3D reasoning requires embodied agents to interpret objects, scene geometry, and viewpoint dependent spatial relations. Existing methods learn grounded interactions from supervised traces, but largely imitate prescribed evidence acquisition patterns rather than optimizing the support that the returned evidence provides for the correct answer. Moreover, outcome rewards provide limited credit for intermediate tool choices and may leave infrequent tools underexplored. An effective agent should instead adaptively decide what to ground, which tool to invoke, and how to assess the utility of returned evidence. To this end, this paper presents CARE-3D, a reinforcement post-training framework for adaptive grounded reasoning. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on grounding instructions first establishes valid interactions, after which Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) optimizes the agent while keeping the 3D grounding module frozen. CARE-3D combines Counterfactual Attribution of Returned Evidence for evidence sensitive credit assignment, and Group Coverage Sampling to preserve tool coverage. Experiments on MSQA and Beacon3D show consistent gains over SFT and GRPO using only answer and format rewards, especially in spatial reasoning and grounding answer coherence. Our code is available at https://github.com/xiaoqian-UQ/CARE-3D{CARE-3D}.

title: GOLD-SLAM: Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM
text: Panoramic cameras capture nearly the entire spherical field of view in a single frame. However, the mismatch between this panoramic coverage and the field of view of LiDAR poses a substantial challenge for panoramic Gaussian splatting SLAM that relies on LiDAR depth priors. We introduce GOLD-SLAM, a Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM system that combines high-quality rendering with accurate geometric reconstruction. It performs tracking and mapping in the spherical domain and uses tracked visual features in regions without LiDAR coverage to improve pose estimation. To address insufficient coverage of newly observed surfaces and floating artifacts during incremental mapping, we introduce Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP). To enable broader evaluation, we collect a new dataset, WHOLE, using a UAV platform across Weak-geometry, High-dynamic, Omnidirectional, Low-light, and Easy scenarios. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and WHOLE demonstrate competitive rendering quality and improved geometric accuracy relative to perspective systems. Compared with existing panoramic baselines, GOLD-SLAM improves mean PSNR by 5.56-9.10 dB and reduces mean Depth-L1 by 71.9-83.9%. To assess deployment feasibility on resource-constrained platforms such as UAVs, we evaluate an embedded configuration of GOLD-SLAM on a Jetson Orin NX (16 GB), demonstrating online operation at the cost of reconstruction quality.

title: Simulator-as-Proxy World Model for Robot Manipulation
text: Video world models for robots are increasingly conditioned on a simulated or rendered proxy of the scene, on the assumption that the video will show what the proxy shows. Testing this assumption requires a proxy whose state is explicit and can be perturbed. We present SimPWM (Simulator-as-Proxy World Model): given a calibrated camera, it represents, from the first frame alone, the robot by its 3D model and the objects the gripper may touch as 3D points; a rule-based simulator with no trained parameters moves them under the actions, and a video model renders the result. SimPWM returns the realistic video together with the simulated state. We then freeze the simulated objects while the arm moves as recorded and check whether the video still shows the object lifted. On DROID episodes from unseen setups, the answer differs for the arm and for the objects. With each of three base video models, the arm follows the proxy (robot IoU 0.75-0.78, against at most 0.69 for end-to-end models); rendering the robot alone already gives this. What the simulated objects add is the object state: against a robot-only proxy, they cut missed pick-ups from 54% to 38%, and the video follows them only with some base models: on rigid objects, freezing them lowers the lift rate of MiniMax-H3, fine-tuned on episodes whose simulation agrees with the real video, from 42% to 10%, but that of LTX-2.3, trained on the same episodes, only from 57% to 49%, as if it inferred the grasp from the arm motion; more than half of the remaining lifts of MiniMax-H3 are of cloth and rope, which the simulator carries rigidly. With any base model, the simulated state records what the simulation did; under perturbed actions, a video that disagrees with it reveals that the video ignores the simulated state.

title: A Mesh for Every Moment
text: We present MEMO (a Mesh for Every MOment), a method that reconstructs the geometry of complete dynamic scenes, captured by multiple synchronized cameras, and extracts a mesh at every frame. Existing dynamic Gaussian splatting methods either model appearance alone or target isolated objects segmented by foreground masks, and all of them recover meshes by TSDF fusion or Poisson reconstruction, whose fixed grids limit the detail they can capture. At the core of MEMO is a per-Gaussian motion model inspired by Gaussian processes, which represents each Gaussian's position and rotation over time as a combination of temporal Gaussian kernels. The model keeps every Gaussian a valid surface element throughout the sequence and carries an implicit representation of the dynamic geometry, so a mesh can be derived at any time from a field defined by the Gaussians. Although common in real captures, large and fast motion poses a challenge that dynamic Gaussian splatting methods usually overlook. To account for it, we design a track-based initialization scheme that fits each Gaussian's initial trajectory to point tracks in closed form. We evaluate MEMO on Blender-Moments, a new benchmark of nine animated scenes with ground-truth meshes at every frame, and on two real-world datasets. MEMO reconstructs the most accurate geometry among state-of-the-art methods, and remains competitive in novel-view synthesis and training time. Project page: https://memo-4d.github.io

title: SOLVE: Sparse, Ordered Keyposes Make LLM Agents Versatile and Efficient Robot Manipulator
text: LLM agents have made remarkable progress in robot manipulation, yet they suffer from expensive inference, dense step-by-step control, and tool bottlenecks. We introduce SOLVE, a training-free, versatile and efficient agent policy: a multimodal LLM agent writes a sparse, ordered sequence of 6-DoF end-effector keyposes per call, observes the result, and writes the next, while a motion planner interpolates between them. The agent decides the number and spacing of keyposes for both fast long-range motion and fine-grained manipulation. This granularity matches the sparsity of teleoperated manipulation: most demonstrations in DROID can be compressed into a few keyposes instead of dense actions. SOLVE grounds keyposes with sparse depth queries answered by noisy sources, such as multi-view triangulation, stereo, or monocular depth, and copes with that noise itself. It also improves from execution feedback, reflecting on its own rollouts and distilling a few rules per task. SOLVE reaches state-of-the-art performance of 74.5% on RoboDojo and 84.5% on RoboLab, with only $1.7 per episode on average, 12x less than previous dense-control agent policies. On a real robot, the same agent achieves an 88% success rate (75 of 85 episodes) over 16 challenging zero-shot tasks. Our project page is at https://serenos.github.io/solve-website.

title: OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms
text: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.8 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes.

title: Stable Gated DeltaNet-2: Understanding and Mitigating Recurrent State Instability
text: Linear attention offers an efficient solution for long-sequence modeling via linear complexity and fixed-size recurrent states. Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) introduces independent channel-wise control over erasure and writing, enhancing state-update expressiveness and in-context retrieval, yet it suffers from training failures during long-context training. We trace these failures to the asymmetry between reading and modification directions during erasure, which yields non-normal erase operators whose directional gains accumulate across tokens, triggering exponential state growth even without new writes. To resolve this, we propose , employing symmetric erasure to ensure non-expansive state propagation and decay-regulated residual writing to preserve writing flexibility. Theoretically, we establish an O(T) upper bound on recurrent state growth while retaining chunkwise parallel computation. Experiments on ~1.6B parameter models show that achieves stable training alongside improved long-context retrieval. Compared to GDN-2, it boosts the 128K average RULER score by 6.80 points in the recurrent setting and average accuracy across nine downstream tasks by 0.62 points in the hybrid setting.

title: ProxyGenBench: Benchmarking Proxy-Guided Video Generation
text: Recent video generators produce realistic videos, yet controlling how scenes unfold remains challenging. Structural proxies, such as animated 3D blockouts, guide generation by specifying scene layout, motion, camera behavior, and event order. However, these coarse inputs leave details unspecified and may contain artifacts that should not be reproduced. Successful proxy-guided generation must therefore Preserve intended structure, Complete missing content and correct proxy artifacts, and Bind text, image, and audio conditions to the right entities and events. We introduce ProxyGenBench to study these interacting requirements, with 312 evaluation cases from 60 scenes across three scene tasks and controlled variations in proxy fidelity, text detail, and multimodal inputs. We evaluate five video generators using verified, case-specific checklists. Experiments show that proxies improve spatiotemporal control, but greater proxy detail can coincide with poorer completion, while strong structural adherence does not ensure correct binding.

title: What a Forecasting Leaderboard Can Establish: Resolution Reporting for Zero-Shot Time-Series Models
text: A foundation model for time series is pretrained once and then asked to forecast series it has never seen, so the evidence for it is its score on held-out datasets. Such datasets are scarce, and a few public leaderboards carry most comparisons, yet none of them states how small a difference its datasets can detect. We call that quantity the resolution of a board and introduce Vernier, a tool that computes it from the files a board already publishes. Vernier also reports which entries a board cannot separate from its leader and whether its order changes when unrelated parties submit. GIFT-Eval resolves 6.8 rank places, and its displayed neighbours sit 0.91 apart. The ten places of its top ten hold fewer than two resolvable steps. fev-bench, Chronos Benchmark II and TIME show the same pattern: their resolution is 3.6 to 19 times the gap between neighbours. With each of its 2,554 series as an independent source, BOOM is the one board that resolves its top ten. Below the resolution the order depends on who else submitted: across four boards, rules that rank against the pool reversed 43 top-ten pairs with neither entry rerun, in one update in seven. Boards also do not record how much history a model receives. On 70 configurations, shortening it raised the error of three of four open models, two of them by 15%. We release Vernier, which runs this report with one command on any leaderboard that publishes per-dataset scores: https://github.com/therealram18/vernier

title: StateWeaver: Multi-Agent Coordination of Story-State Transitions for Long-Horizon Video Generation
text: Modern video foundation models generate high-quality short clips, but preserving long-video consistency and correctly depicting event-driven state changes remain challenging. Existing agentic workflows face these challenges because continual planning and repair accumulate context, while reference updates remain limited. We introduce StateWeaver, which combines Active States and Hierarchical Collaboration to connect review-driven visual reference updates with cross-shot state inheritance. Active States translate state discrepancies identified during review into concrete visual asset requirements that guide reference construction, validation, and regeneration, preserving identity and already-correct content while repairing target attributes. Confirmed generation results are linked to the corresponding asset states, story time, and reference versions for verification and reuse by subsequent shots. Hierarchical Collaboration isolates execution contexts by task, clip, and repair round, and uses hierarchical memory to organize this process across multiple sets. Across multiple benchmarks, StateWeaver outperforms existing methods and produces long videos with sustained cross-shot consistency under predefined and autonomously planned storyboards.

title: ShowNow: Fine-Grained Speculative Streaming for Responsive World Models
text: Interactive world models must generate video continuously while responding promptly to user actions. Real-time throughput alone leaves input latency unresolved: coarse generation blocks delay action updates, and generation after input adds work to the response path. We introduce ShowNow, a fine-grained speculative streaming framework that uses computation available during playback to prepare action-conditioned futures before input arrives. Single-latent commitment enables frequent decisions, while configurable preparation covers one to eight actions. We construct a matched multi-future dataset to train alternative continuations from a common state; shared-history tree execution and fused commitment make their preparation efficient. On a single H100, our 5B model sustains 480p generation at 16 fps with eight prepared futures. In ViZDoom, the complete ShowNow deployment reduces median input-to-display latency from 620 to 208 ms relative to the native-block SolarWM-FT deployment. Matched-policy experiments reduce restart empty ticks from 1.56% to 0.09% (94%) and improve on-time responses to action changes. These results establish complementary roles for fine-grained commitment and advance preparation, with measured trade-offs in visual fidelity and long-horizon consistency. ShowNow turns playback-time computation into responsive visual interaction. Project: https://github.com/showlab/ShowNow.

title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
text: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

title: Solve Vision with Code: Coding Agents Are Stronger Visual Reasoners Than Video Models
text: Video generation models are increasingly evaluated as visual reasoners: given a first frame and a natural-language prompt, can the model produce the video in which the specified task is carried out? The paradigm is considered advantageous because the reasoning is native to the visual medium, unfolding directly in the frames rather than through language or code. Whether this native route is in fact the more reliable path to visual reasoning has not been tested against a symbolic alternative under the same conditions. We therefore pose the same tasks, with identical inputs, output specification and evaluator, to both media: rather than denoising pixels, a coding agent writes a program that renders the answer video, which an unmodified rule-based evaluator scores. On VBVR-Pro-Bench (Xu et al., 2026), a 500-instance suite spanning five cognitive categories with symbolic ground truth, the agent receives the same first frame and prompt as the video model, with no access to ground truth, metadata or generation models, and one attempt per instance. Three closed-model agents (Codex with gpt-6-astra, Claude Code with Fable 5.1 and Gemini CLI with Gemini 3.1 Pro) score 0.923, 0.894 and 0.893, each more than 0.22 above the strongest video model. Among 23 runnable open-weight models, the best, GLM-5, reaches 0.572, above all video models except the RL-trained one. Together, we show that for tasks whose solutions can be computed from a first frame and a prompt, program synthesis is currently a substantially more reliable route to visual reasoning than video generation. We further distinguish depictive programs, which navigate the image to recover a transferable scheme, from propositional programs, which operate on hard-coded values, revealing how visual reasoning unfolds in agent-written programs and what it implies for its nature of reasoning in general.

title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation
text: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.

title: When an AI agent makes a mistake in a database, what decides the damage?
text: AI agents now run statements against production databases, and several of the incidents that followed deleted production data, which came back only through backups or the provider's help. We ask what decides the damage when such an agent makes a mistake: the model, a guard layer in front of the database, or the database engine itself. The study has two preregistered layers. In Layer A, a frozen library of 22 canonical mistakes is applied by script, with no model involved, to four relational engines under five permission arms and two recovery arms, followed by an engine-native recovery drill (792 cells; 874 drill runs including 10-minute repeats). In Layer B, a minimal tool-calling agent driven by six small open-weight models (4B to 12B parameters, plus one 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B active, served locally) works on tasks that contain hazards across nine engines: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, ClickHouse, Apache Cassandra, MongoDB, Valkey, Apache Kafka and OpenSearch (9,468 trials). A secondary run added MariaDB, Redis and Elasticsearch (2,916 trials); each behaved like its closest core engine. Out of the box, the engines differ less in what a mistake destroys than in what they let you undo. Three of the seven preregistered hypotheses met their decision rule: H2 (for one of nine damage classes) and H3 largely by construction of the arms, and H4 only under its original measure. Four did not; one of them (H5) was uninformative, because in its task the agents never found the credential. The post-hoc analyses (S1-S13) are exploratory and uncorrected for multiple comparisons; on PostgreSQL, MySQL, OpenSearch and ClickHouse the preregistered outcome and original-row loss disagree about G1. We report all of them, with every deviation from the preregistration and its timing.

title: Reading, Not Adapting: Unlocking Frozen Visual Knowledge for AI-Generated Image Detection
text: Generalization to unseen image generators has driven efforts to adapt pretrained visual representations for detection. Yet recent findings show that vision foundation models already encode transferable detection knowledge, while further adaptation can impair generalization. This motivates a shift from backbone adaptation to knowledge readout. Conventional linear probing offers a direct way to read this knowledge but is limited to final-layer RGB features. Multi-cue detectors broaden the evidence base, but their designs introduce other tradeoffs: adaptation may compromise pretrained transferability, heterogeneous encoders complicate feature integration, and late fusion precludes intermediate cross-view interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose ReMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers-inspired framework that reads complementary knowledge from spatially aligned RGB and wavelet views within a fully frozen visual foundation. ReMoT employs staged joint attention to enable controlled local and global cross-view interaction, while learnable fusion queries progressively read complementary evidence across Transformer depth without writeback. ReMoT achieves 91.2% average accuracy across eight benchmark groups with 3,074 trainable parameters, attaining the highest overall average among the evaluated methods. These results support structured knowledge readout as a promising alternative to backbone adaptation. Code is available at https://github.com/yunncheng/ReMoT.

title: Guarding with Judgment: Learning to Intervene for Multimodal Safety
text: When visual context makes an ordinary request unsafe to answer as asked, a blanket refusal may leave the user's need unresolved. Choosing how to help requires distinguishing an established hazard from a condition that still needs verification, a distinction that binary safety labels leave unspecified. We formulate this decision through four actions: allow, warn, review, and refuse. To ground these decisions in verifiable evidence, we build a corpus of 20,126 training audits and the JudiBench benchmark, connecting each action to diagnostic judgments, source evidence, and controlled context changes. Our guard, JudiAct, separately states what the source establishes, what condition governs the help, and how the rules apply. It then checks these three brief review items against the original inputs to predict diagnostic labels and a handling action. Supervised training learns individual judgments while comparing label assignments across related cases. A second stage swaps one review item at a time, using the resulting audit feedback to refine review generation. On JudiBench, JudiAct improves request and answer Macro-F1 by more than 28 percentage points over its 4B backbone. Across nine public benchmarks, it outperforms state-of-the-art guards on the mean delivered-answer score in both pre-generation and post-generation settings, cutting MM-SafetyBench attack success from 40.78% to 25.30%.

title: Generation as Reverse Encoding
text: Pretrained visual representations accelerate generative learning by abstracting away appearance and spatial detail. Yet the same abstraction makes the return to pixels far harder, shifting much of the burden onto a larger decoder. We ask why the representation-to-pixel path should be learned independently when the encoder already provides a learned pixel-to-semantics path (the semantic encoding path). We introduce RevFlow, based on the principle of generation as reverse encoding. RevFlow uses intermediate representations of a frozen encoder as successive generative targets, first generating deep semantic representations, then shallow representations that retain appearance and spatial detail, before decoding to pixels. To learn these transitions without training a separate generator for each stage, we develop HyC-DiT, a unified generative model with a standard DiT backbone shared across stages and stage-specific condition injection. We further show that native matching in semantic representation space enables few-step generation. RevFlow accelerates both learning and sampling. On ImageNet 256 times 256, RevFlow reaches 1.96 FID at 690M and 1.74 FID at 1.55B after only 5 training epochs. It also achieves 30.25 dB reconstruction PSNR with an 89M decoder. After a short native-matching adaptation phase, RevFlow-XL achieves 2.85 FID using a single sampling step in each stage. Our code repository is at https://github.com/ChengShiest/RevFlow

title: Decision-Native Multimodal Clinical Modeling via Anatomical Grounding and Confidence Calibration
text: Structured clinical decisions from volumetric computed tomography (CT) require anatomically grounded predictions and calibrated confidence estimates. However, existing 3D medical multimodal models often suffer from uncalibrated autoregressive decoding and shortcut reliance on irrelevant anatomical regions. We introduce Radev, a decision-native multimodal model that integrates anatomy-guided visual compression, direct candidate prediction, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To bridge global context with fine-grained slice details, a frozen 3D encoder extracts reusable organ-level features, which are dynamically selected by the query to attend to 2D slice features within predicted anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual tokens enable the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. We further propose Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) to compare predictions under intact and intervened organ representations. CCT encourages confidence to decrease when removing target-organ evidence degrades decision quality, while penalizing excessive confidence drops under unrelated-organ removal. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, a comprehensive benchmark spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions, and ordinal severity assessment across both in-distribution and external cohorts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Radev significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both decision accuracy and confidence calibration, while generalizing robustly under distribution shifts. Project page at https://juntaojianggavin.github.io/projects/Radev/

title: So Many Ways to Multiply 3times3 Matrices: A Large Dataset of Rank-23 Schemes
text: A publicly available dataset of 62029 rank-23 schemes for 3times3 matrix multiplication is presented. Every scheme in it has its own rank pattern, an invariant formed by the ranks of the factor matrices of a scheme, so all schemes are pairwise inequivalent. The schemes were obtained by a numerical method combining gradient descent with alternating least squares and by flip graph search, and have ternary, integer or rational coefficients. Rank 23 is the best known for this format and is optimal for schemes with integer coefficients, but the number of essentially different schemes of this rank was poorly understood: the existing collections of Heule et al. and Mårtensson et al. contain many schemes that share only a small number of rank patterns (17376 schemes with 387 patterns and 15316 schemes with 568 patterns respectively). The dataset shows that the number of different rank patterns is much larger than previously known.

title: Pretrained Tabular Features and the Measurement of Financial Proximity
text: Spatial arbitrage pricing theory (S-APT) extends factor models to allow returns to spill over between connected firms, beyond what common risk factors explain. In recent years, tabular foundation models (TFMs) have matched or outperformed tuned gradient-boosted and bagged ensembles on small and medium-sized tabular benchmarks. Although their predictive performance is strong, these models reveal little about what they have learned, which limits their use in regulated financial applications that require explanation. Internal representations are widely used to probe what neural networks learn and to measure similarity. In this paper, we use the frozen representations of four TFMs as a measure of financial dissimilarity in a spatial asset-pricing model of US equities from 2011 to 2025, and find that their estimated gains over a direct distance between the same disclosures become consistently positive once broad SEC filing data are included. This reframes tabular foundation models from black-box predictors into instruments for measuring economic structure, with immediate applications to peer selection, risk attribution and network-based asset pricing. More broadly, our findings suggest that the internal representations of foundation models, not only their predictions, deserve study as economic objects, opening a new line of research on what pretrained models know about firms.

An introduction to uncertainty in machine learning
text: An Introduction to Uncertainty in Machine Learning Every model makes an assumption about uncertainty, often without saying so. Where data is rare, that assumption decides the answer. This introduction explains where uncertainty comes from and how to judge when it needs to be faithful to be useful. Essentially, all models are wrong, but some are useful. Most of machine learning is based on probabilistic modelling, even if it does not always seem like it. So most models carry some uncertainty, whether we chose it or not, and in many decisions it pays to take that uncertainty into account, as the examples in this post show. In my experience, uncertainty in machine learning is a confusing topic to get into, so I wrote this introduction to give an intuitive overview. It is not comprehensive, but it should give you a good enough mental model to choose assumptions that make your uncertainty estimates useful for decision making, even though, as Box put it, the model itself will always be wrong.This post is based on a talk I gave at the University of Alicante. The slides are online. For a more thorough introduction, see Chapters 2 and 3 of my PhD thesis . Generally speaking, uncertainty is incomplete knowledge, and probability is how we describe it: a distribution over the possible outcomes says how plausible each one is, given what we know. It helps to separate two kinds of uncertainty: Epistemic uncertainty comes from what we have not learned yet, such as the true relationship between inputs and outputs. More data can reduce it. Aleatoric uncertainty comes from what we cannot observe: the inputs do not determine the outcome, so more data of the same kind will not remove it. The line between the two depends on what we measure. A coin flip follows classical mechanics. If we do not measure how the coin is thrown, the best we can say is 50/50, and the uncertainty is aleatoric. If we do measure it, physics tells us how it will land, and the uncertainty becomes epistemic: now we have to learn the physics, which takes data. Richer inputs can reduce aleatoric uncertainty, but they give the model more to learn, and whether that pays off depends on how much data and prior knowledge we have.Some inputs are out of reach. For example, weather is chaotic, so tiny differences, as small as the flap of a butterfly's wings, can grow into different weather a few weeks later. Since we cannot observe every butterfly, part of the uncertainty in a forecast stays aleatoric, however much we measure. A prediction is not a decision. When we decide, we often weigh the possible outcomes by how likely they are and what they would cost us, including rare outcomes that could hurt us badly. A single number hides this picture. It also cannot tell us when to hand a case to a human or to collect more data before we decide. The examples below show where modelling uncertainty matters. A human decides. The model does not know what is at stake. A 20% chance of rain means one thing for a wedding and another for a walk. The model should therefore tell us how likely rain is, so that each of us can decide what that means for our own plans. A point estimate is not enough. When several outcomes are plausible, a single prediction cannot represent them all. And when rare outcomes are costly, the tail risk can matter more than the typical case, yet a single prediction hides it. We can choose not to decide yet. Selective automation hands unsure cases to a human. This works even for aleatoric uncertainty. If dust and an impurity look the same from the camera’s angle, more labels will not help the model, but a person can turn the part and look again. We can ask for the right data. Active learning and Bayesian optimization use uncertainty to ask for new data where it is most useful. It feeds further computation. title: Who Makes the Decision? Auditing an Agentic LLM Pipeline for Illicit Cryptocurrency Transaction Monitoring
text: Agentic pipelines that combine graph detectors, deterministic rules, retrieval-augmented generation and an LLM judge are being proposed to monitor illicit cryptocurrency flows and to write regulation-citing justifications for analysts. They are evaluated on end-to-end accuracy or on the quality of those justifications, and neither shows which component made a decision. We audit such a pipeline on the Elliptic++ Bitcoin dataset with decision-source attribution, a trace-level protocol with three layers: per-case actual causation, interventional Shapley credit, and mediation of upstream risk scores. A deterministic wallet-score override carries about 94% of the credit for flags, and a verification gate cancels most of the judge's own flags, which fall on licit transactions. Testing the judge alone over 76 evidence bundles, four backbones and two prompts, we find that it follows an injected risk score on the anonymous transaction features it is given, although stronger models decide correctly when the facts are explicit; that a context too short for the system prompt leaves it with no verdict at all; and that it cites regulatory clauses that do not apply, which a substring-based citation check accepts. Hiding the score does not fix the judge, because evidence gathered with the score visible still encodes it. For illicit-activity monitoring, an LLM's justification should therefore not be read as evidence of which component flagged a transaction.

title: Revisiting LLMs as Context Engineers
text: As large language models (LLMs) are used in more and more new tasks, context engineering becomes a fundamental method to efficiently steer LLMs by constructing instruction prompts or metadata without intensive training. A growing number of LLM context engineering (LCE) approaches automate the task by casting the LLM itself as the engineer that draws generalizable instructions or experiences from offline trials as context. Although these methods resemble how humans learn from experiences, it remains unclear when and how LLMs can engineer effective context from data. To answer the question, we first establish a benchmark composed of datasets with different reasoning patterns. We compared different LCE methods with different LLM families in 8B size, showing that there is no single winner for all tasks, even compared with simple baselines like chain-of-thought. Even when scaling model capabilities via more parameters or generation iterations, LCEs do not consistently boost existing performance. Across all datasets and models, the performance gains of LCEs are negatively correlated (r=-0.5, ple 0.05) with the diversity of the failure modes of reasoning trajectories. Investigating how LCEs work, we find that (1) the improvement in instruction adherence can explain some success of LCEs; (2) one major bottleneck is whether LLMs can extract effective experiences out of natively diverse failures. Through this study, we uncover the limited capabilities of LCEs in abstracting principled contexts from diverse failure modes and understand how LCEs work, providing guidelines for future work.

title: Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neurons (DAWIN): A Universal Primitive for Continuous-Time Spatiotemporal Learning
text: Conventional artificial neurons separate spatial feature aggregation from continuous physical time, limiting their ability to model irregular observations. We introduce the Damped Atomic Wave Integration Neuron (DAWIN), a continuous-time primitive for replacing standard neural layers in MLPs, Transformers, and graph neural networks. DAWIN couples spatial projection with elapsed-time-dependent wave excitation and integrates it into a local complex state through closed-form damped evolution, avoiding numerical differential equation solvers. We show that DAWIN generalizes static sinusoidal and memoryless wave neurons on interval-augmented inputs, derive closed-form gradients, and establish bounded-input bounded-output stability for positive damping and sampling intervals bounded away from zero. An associative Triton prefix-scan implementation, DAWINLinear, uses FP32 accumulation and achieves O(log L) parallel depth for sequence length L. Across 11 parameter-matched tasks covering irregular oscillators, MuJoCo dynamics, pedestrian trajectories, and PhysioNet 2012 clinical sequences, DAWIN outperforms Neural CDE on 9 tasks and ReLU-MLP on 8. It achieves the lowest error on dense clinical dynamics (0.9531 NRMSE, winning across all 10 seeds) and ties for the best mortality prediction (0.9993 AUROC). Shuffling elapsed intervals increases error by 58.2%-77.4% on selected dynamics tasks, versus 0.06% on a time-irrelevant control, supporting reliance on physical timing. On NVIDIA B200 GPUs, parallel wave integration accelerates inference by up to 2,630 times over its serial implementation and reduces peak GPU memory by up to 97.6% relative to Mamba in the tested configurations.

title: BiSAT: Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization for Speech Language Models
text: Speech language models (LMs) generate speech as sequences of discrete tokens. Their tokenizer must therefore preserve both acoustic detail and linguistic content at a low bitrate. Semantic-enhanced tokenizers may lose acoustic detail, whereas acoustic-oriented tokenizers retain acoustic variation that makes language modeling harder. Unified tokenizers combine both, but representing acoustic detail and linguistic content within a single feature space can cause interference between the two objectives, and existing approaches typically align acoustic representations to fixed semantic targets from a frozen teacher. We propose Bidirectionally Aligned Semantic-Acoustic Tokenization (BiSAT), a unified tokenization framework with separate acoustic and semantic branches aligned by a shared-index mechanism. This design learns acoustic and semantic representations in separate continuous spaces while producing a single discrete code sequence, and it jointly optimizes both encoders without relying on fixed semantic teacher targets. Based on BiSAT, we develop BiSAT-TTS, a zero-shot text-to-speech system comprising an autoregressive text-speech LM and a conditional flow-matching acoustic decoder. Reconstruction, downstream understanding, and diagnostic analyses show that BiSAT effectively preserves semantic and acoustic information in the code stream, performs well on in-the-wild and out-of-domain speech, and learns complementary codebook representations. The frozen-code understanding results also support its feasibility and potential for code-based reward modeling in reinforcement learning post-training. BiSAT-TTS performs comparably to state-of-the-art speech LM-based TTS baselines with less training data, further supporting BiSAT's effectiveness for speech language modeling. The audio demos are available at https://seekmind-lab.github.io/bisat-demo.

title: Markdown Is Not a Firewall: four coding agents, one rules file, four boundaries
text: Teams put a one-page rules file in a repository and call it a control on coding agents. A registered study found agents rarely look up a repository's contribution rules. I asked the security question: what does a rules file do at a boundary, against a gate? I tested one 278-word rules file, with hypotheses and analysis code deposited first. Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI and OpenCode with DeepSeek worked through 20 small repositories with hidden tests, 12 for three of them. Three agents met four boundaries I built: a refused endpoint, a destructive shortcut, a planted instruction and a planted package. Permission prompts, each vendor's own control layer, were off by design. A gate in front of the mock service blocked and logged forbidden requests. Every verdict was read from records the agent could not change. Only my first scoring pass was blind to arm. My checkers found no real bugs, with the file or without it. The file cost one agent a third of its score: Codex CLI fell from 99.0 to 67.7 percent on hidden tests, and in 11 of its 36 steps reported the task complete with all tests passing while under half of the hidden tests passed. Its own tests passed. Faced with two of its rules that clash on these tasks, three agents followed the task and one followed the rule. Pooled, passes fell from 98.2 to 90.9 percent. Matched pairs fell 7.7 points, 1.3 without Codex CLI. Attempts to cross were rare: 5 in 90 gated steps, 3 without the file, 2 with it, all by OpenCode with DeepSeek, all blocked. With no gate, under the neutral file, the same requests reached the mock in 7 of 45 runs. By an error in my run script, the no-file and rules-file arms always ran behind the gate at the three HTTP boundaries, so I could not test whether the file changes what an agent does there. On what I could measure, the file acted as advice. A file tells an agent what you want. A gate decides what it gets.

title: InitFree-SfM: When Initialization-Free Bundle Adjustment meets Learned Structure-from-Motion
text: Initialization-free bundle adjustment (InitFree BA) aims to jointly recover camera poses and scene structure without requiring an initial global estimate. It is a very challenging problem, especially compared to traditional BA where a good estimation is assumed. While recent methods optimize surrogate Object Space Error (OSE) objectives from random initialization, a low objective value does not necessarily yield an accurate reconstruction, revealing a gap between optimization and reconstruction. We show that existing InitFree BA pipelines struggle to produce accurate 3D reconstructions on modern SfM benchmarks, and demonstrate that incorporating learned metric depth substantially improves their practical feasibility. We introduce InitFree-SfM, a complete initialization-free SfM pipeline combining learned correspondences, metric depth, depth-consistent track construction, and joint metric refinement. Within this framework, we propose a simple depth-augmented OSE (dOSE), which complements the directional constraints of OSE by constraining landmark positions along their viewing rays. Our approach substantially outperforms existing InitFree BA methods and achieves competitive accuracy with established SfM pipelines, including on challenging low-overlap image collections. Importantly, our analysis challenges the prevailing emphasis on surrogate objectives in previous InitFree BA research, revealing that geometric constraints play a central role in accurate reconstruction, while OSE-based optimization provides further improvements.

title: Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5
text: Taking Trainium3 to the Track: Generating Videos with LTX-2.5 Thanks to our partnership with AWS, we were lucky enough to get access to a Trainium3 machine (trn3.48xlarge, 64 NeuronCores) for a month. We spent most of the month testing Hugging Face models on it, and getting more of them to work. With five days left, I allowed myself a little fun. When you have a Ferrari, every now and then you want to take it out on the track. So I asked myself: what if I tried to generate videos? I picked LTX-2.5 from Lightricks, which generates video and sound together. By the end, once the models were loaded, a 10-second clip with sound took 22 to 23 s to generate, on half of the machine. Here is the result. I had two goals. The first was to see how easy it is to generate videos with diffusers on Trainium3. Not the simple clips from the examples: I wanted to make short films from a script, closer to a real use case, like drafting a movie. The second was performance. I wanted to get close to what you get with CUDA, or with LTX's own API. For CUDA, I found no real figure to compare against. The only one is LTX's claim of 6.8 s for a 10-second 720p clip on four B200 GPUs, with no detail on how it was measured. So I set CUDA aside and compared with LTX's online API instead, which LTX says makes a 10-second 1080p clip in 23.7 s. In the end, the setup matches it, and even beats it by about a second: 22 to 23 s for a 10-second clip at 2048×1024, once the models are loaded, on half of the machine. Not bad, considering how little time I had to optimize the pipelines. The input is a film: a JSON list of shots, each with a name and a prompt, much like a storyboard. LTX-2.5 does better with long prompts, so each prompt is a paragraph on the style, the subject, the motion, the camera, the light and the sound. Here is the seal film's file, with the prompts shortened: Each shot has a name and a prompt, and can have a seed, to keep the take I picked among several. Shots are chained with two keys. This chaining is the point, since prompts alone do not keep a subject from one shot to the next: from: the shot starts from the last frames of an earlier shot. Starting from the earlier shot's last frame keeps a subject's look across a cut; starting from its last 25 frames (1 s) also continues the motion. to: the shot ends on the first frames of a later shot, so that it leads into it. A shot can also be trimmed, or have a caption drawn over it. Making a film from shots works like animation, which has two ways to go. Straight ahead, each shot continues the one before. Pose to pose, you make the key shot first, until you get one you like; then the shots before it end on its first frames (to), and the shots after it start from its last frames (from). When a film builds up to a payoff (the moment everything was leading to), the payoff is the key shot. I found this order by trial and error, and made the seal film pose to pose, starting from iceberg. The payoff is iceberg: the iceberg rolls over, and its wave drenches the seal. nap, the sleeping seal, ends on the first 9 frames of iceberg (to), so that the seal, the floe and the iceberg stay the same into the payoff. shake starts from the last 25 frames of iceberg (from): the dripping seal shakes off the water and flops down on the floe. The dream is made on its own, and a cut joins it to the rest. On the diffusers side, three pipelines share the models of LTX-2.5. LTX2Pipeline makes the shots from their prompt alone, and LTX2ConditionPipeline makes the shots that start or end on frames of another shot. These two follow the two-stage distilled recipe of the model card: 8 steps, then the third pipeline, LTX2LatentUpsamplePipeline, upscales the latents ×2 before 3 final steps. The diffusers pipelines do all of the generation. title: States sue SpaceX to stop Grok from generating child sex images, revenge porn
text: Commonwealth of Virginia Office of the Attorney General 202 North 9th Street Richmond, Virginia 23219 804-786-2071 FAX 804-786-1991 Virginia Relay Service 800-828-1120 For media inquiries only, contact: Rae Pickett RPickett@oag.state.va.us Attorneys General Jones and Rayfield File Suit Against SpaceX, Parent Company of X, xAI, and Grok, Over Creation and Promotion of Child Exploitation and Non-Consensual Images on Platform Virginia and Oregon Attorneys General seek accountability for harms and significant new protections for consumers RICHMOND, Va. – Today, Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones took a significant step in holding operators of X and its AI tool, Grok, accountable for knowingly failing to protect Virginians, while falsely promoting the safety of its platform and AI tool. Today’s suit was filed in collaboration with Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield, who filed a separate but similar action. “This lawsuit is about seeking justice for the millions of Virginians who maintain accounts on X and were misled by the company’s false reassurances that their data and images would be safe on the platform,” said Virginia Attorney General Jay Jones. “When xAI allowed Grok’s creators to sideline consent to turn a profit, they prioritized growth and engagement over safety, and they deceived the public about it. Today’s filings are the first step towards holding this company accountable.” With a single existing photograph, Grok could, and did, fabricate a realistic image or video of a person nude, or partially nude, or engaged in sexual activity, all without the individual’s knowledge or consent. There’s a growing sense in the AI community that we’re approaching an intelligence explosion far faster than even the most optimistic accelerationists predicted. One of the most publicly visible signals pointing at that acceleration is the rapid progress made in mathematics in recent months. Navier-Stokes, one of the central Millennium Prize Problems posed by the Clay Mathematics Institute more than a quarter century ago, fell in September. Last Friday, Anthropic researcher and mathematician Levent Alpöge announced a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis, which paradoxically can be verified using a mathematics program called Lean, but has yet to be understood by human experts. Just last night, Anthropic casually posted a solution to the VP vs VNP problem without any fanfare. Such things are becoming the norm. Because mathematics is deterministic, though, observers have wondered whether this same process of research and discovery will generalize to non-deterministic domains like history. In this blog post, I will present evidence that this is indeed starting to happen. I recently had the opportunity to test OpenAI’s new model, GPT-6.2 Astra, before it was released and it made a significant historical discovery. This required it to read through sources, develop a hypothesis with limited evidence, and make an argument. Moreover, it would be unlikely that a human could replicate what it did. With only minimal prompting, GPT-6.2 Astra was able to autonomously identify the creator of an anonymous 1808 sketchbook held at Yale’s Beinecke Library. It did so extremely quickly (in just 22 minutes), using publicly available primary and secondary sources. To do so, it discovered a little known source in a paper archive, predicted that it would prove its hypothesis if examined and, in the end, it did. Not only that, but this new source turns out to be a major find on its own that will be of significant interest to both Canadian and fur trade historians. While it’s a narrow example, it’s representative of the historical research process as a whole and a sign of things to come. I started testing GPT-6.2 Astra in late October in the ChatGPT Windows Desktop app. It is a quirky but highly capable model, especially well suited to long-running, open-ended tasks that might take hours or days to complete. In essence, it tested the handwritten math across thousands of quantities, item prices, sub-totals and account totals over the course of only a few hours and made edits accordingly. I had previously tried this with both GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5 and neither one completed the task as thoroughly or competently. Even so, GPT-6.2 Astra sometimes communicates in a weird way, writing backwards-speak, riddle-like answers that seem wrong at first glance but turn out to be technically correct. It often feels like I’m reading a formal legal disclaimer, but one written in a friendly, colloquial way. The strangest thing, though, is that the underlying work product is always sound. Then 100x builds a small model that runs your real functions, and a checker visits every state the model can reach. When something breaks, it prints the shortest list of steps that gets there. Small blocks add up to a big system Each block is checked on its own, so a failure points at one small thing. The seams are checked too: what one block hands over has to meet the next block's rules. Then the real blocks run together in one model, and the checker visits every state of the whole. Checked blocks plus checked seams add up to software you can trust. The blocks do not prove the seams for free, so 100x checks both. It stays true The ledger is verify/ledger.tsv, in your repo, so it travels with every branch. Each row keeps a hash of the code it covers. Change that code and the row goes stale until someone reads the change, runs the check and syncs it. Every property has to fail once on a planted bug before it counts. 100x finish refuses a property that is stale, broken or never failed. When an agent is about to touch code that no rule covers, 100x verify cover answers NO RULE, and that starts the procedure. Each round looks at the project in a new way, keeps the change if it helped, and rolls it back if it didn't. A fresh second model checks every round. FAQ Why a second model? Different models have different blind spots. If none is available, the run still finishes and says UNREVIEWED. On a single plan, a smaller model from the same company can judge, with less benefit than another company's model. Will it put my project online? No. It makes a preview only if the project already has one. Going live needs you to say so. What if I hit a usage limit mid-run? 100x saves progress in .100x/STATE.md. When the limit resets, type /100x-continue in the same folder. Does it change my model or settings? No. It never switches your model, effort level or sign-in. /100x-setup only writes 100x's own settings. Where do runs live? In a hidden .100x/ folder in each project (git ignores it), and a gallery of finished runs in ~/.100x.
